cards.title: From Freytag's pyramid to the six shapes of stories
cards.summary: In Die Technik des Dramas (1863), the German novelist and playwright Gustav Freytag analysed five-act tragedies, especially Shakespeare and Greek drama, and described a dramatic structure now taught as Freytag's pyramid: exposition, rising action, climax, falling action and catastrophe or denouement. The model was built for tragedy and fits many modern stories imperfectly, but it gives writers a vocabulary for tension, turning points and release. A century later, Kurt Vonnegut proposed a more playful approach. In a lecture later included in his collection Palm Sunday (1981), and drawing on a master's thesis he said the University of Chicago had rejected, he plotted stories on a graph of good fortune against time. Man in Hole falls into trouble and climbs out; Boy Meets Girl gains, loses and regains; Cinderella rises, falls and then rises higher. In 2016 a team at the University of Vermont, led by Andrew Reagan, tested a version of this idea using sentiment analysis on more than 1,300 works of fiction from Project Gutenberg. They found that emotional trajectories cluster into six basic shapes: rags to riches, riches to rags, man in a hole, Icarus, Cinderella and Oedipus. They also found that some shapes, such as Icarus and Oedipus, were associated with more downloads, suggesting audiences enjoy particular combinations of rise and fall.
cards.deepDive: Sentiment-based story arcs have limits: measuring the emotional tone of words is not the same as measuring plot, and literary scholars have criticised computational studies for oversimplification. Matthew Jockers's Syuzhet package sparked a similar debate in 2015, when Annie Swafford pointed out technical problems with its smoothing method. These debates are a good introduction to the field of digital humanities and its promise and pitfalls.

cards.title: The hero's journey and its critics
cards.summary: Joseph Campbell's The Hero with a Thousand Faces (1949) argued that myths from around the world share a common pattern, which he called the monomyth. Drawing on comparative mythology and Jungian psychology, Campbell described a hero who receives a call to adventure, often refuses it, crosses a threshold into an unknown world with the help of a mentor, faces trials, undergoes a supreme ordeal, gains a reward and returns transformed, bringing a boon to the community. His summary formula: a hero ventures from the common world into a region of supernatural wonder, wins a decisive victory and comes back with the power to bestow benefits on others. George Lucas said Campbell's work influenced Star Wars, and in the 1980s Christopher Vogler, a Hollywood story analyst, wrote a memo for Disney adapting Campbell into a twelve-stage template later published as The Writer's Journey. The structure has since shaped countless films and novels. Critics argue that Campbell selected and flattened his examples to fit the pattern, ignored myths that do not fit, centred male heroes and treated non-Western traditions superficially. Folklorists generally prefer more empirical approaches. For writers, the monomyth is best treated as one useful pattern among many rather than a universal law of storytelling.
cards.deepDive: A more rigorous precursor is Vladimir Propp's Morphology of the Folktale (1928), which analysed a defined corpus of Russian fairy tales rather than all world myth. The folklorist Alan Dundes was a sharp critic of Campbell's method. Maureen Murdock's The Heroine's Journey (1990) was written partly as a response to the male focus of Campbell's model.

cards.title: Propp's 31 functions: the grammar of fairy tales
cards.summary: In Morphology of the Folktale, published in Russian in 1928 and translated into English in 1958, the Soviet folklorist Vladimir Propp analysed 100 Russian wonder tales from Alexander Afanasyev's collection. Instead of classifying tales by theme or character, as earlier folklorists had done, Propp focused on what characters do in the plot. He identified 31 functions, recurring narrative actions that always appear in the same order, though not every tale contains all of them. They include absentation, a family member leaves home; interdiction, the hero is warned; violation of the interdiction; villainy or lack; the hero's departure; testing by a donor; the acquisition of a magical agent; struggle with the villain; victory; return; pursuit; rescue; the unrecognised arrival; a false hero's claim; a difficult task; recognition; exposure of the false hero; and finally wedding. He also identified seven character roles, or spheres of action: the villain, the donor, the helper, the princess and her father, the dispatcher, the hero and the false hero. Propp's key insight was that the functions are stable while the characters filling them change. A dragon, witch or tsar can all be the villain. The book became foundational for structuralism, narratology and later for computational storytelling and game design.
cards.deepDive: Propp's work became internationally influential only after its 1958 English translation, when structuralists such as Claude Lévi-Strauss engaged with it, sometimes critically. A. J. Greimas reduced Propp's roles to an actantial model of six positions: subject, object, sender, receiver, helper and opponent. Researchers in artificial intelligence have used Proppian functions as a grammar for automated story generation.

cards.title: Free indirect style: the novel's great invention
cards.summary: Free indirect discourse, or free indirect style, is a way of narrating that blends a third-person narrator's voice with a character's thoughts, without quotation marks or tags like she thought. Compare she thought, I will be late again, with: She would be late again, of course. The second sentence is grammatically the narrator's, yet the of course belongs to the character. The technique lets a writer move fluidly between inside and outside, sympathy and irony, in a way that drama and first-person narration cannot easily manage. Jane Austen is often credited with perfecting it in English, notably in Emma (1815), where the reader sees events through Emma's misjudgements while the narrator quietly signals they are mistaken. Gustave Flaubert made it central to Madame Bovary (1856), and the trial of the book for offending public morals partly turned on whether the narrator or Emma was responsible for its sensuous passages. In How Fiction Works (2008), the critic James Wood argues that free indirect style is the novel's defining technique, because it allows a story to be told simultaneously through a character's eyes and language and through an author's eyes and language. Once you notice it, you will see it on nearly every page of modern fiction, from Henry James to Sally Rooney.
cards.deepDive: Linguists and narratologists have studied the grammar of free indirect style closely; Ann Banfield's Unspeakable Sentences (1982) argued that some of its sentences cannot be spoken by anyone, a provocative claim about narration. Dorrit Cohn's Transparent Minds (1978) is the classic survey of how fiction presents consciousness, including psycho-narration, quoted monologue and narrated monologue, her term for free indirect style.

cards.title: Chekhov's gun: every detail is a promise
cards.summary: Chekhov's gun is the dramatic principle that every element introduced into a story should be necessary, and that details which are emphasised should eventually pay off. It is named after Anton Chekhov, who expressed the idea in several forms in letters and conversations. The best-known version, recorded by acquaintances, says roughly that if you show a rifle hanging on the wall in the first act, it must go off by the third act, and if it is not going to be fired, it should not be hanging there. Chekhov's point was about economy: audiences and readers treat what is foregrounded as significant, so a writer who introduces unused elements breaks an implicit promise. Chekhov's own plays illustrate this, sometimes literally. In The Seagull a gun appears and is fired, and Uncle Vanya contains a pistol scene. The principle connects to foreshadowing and setup-and-payoff, which screenwriters treat as essential. It also has interesting tensions. Mystery writers deliberately use red herrings, details that look significant but mislead. Realist novelists sometimes include incidental details to create a sense of reality, which the critic Roland Barthes called the reality effect. Good writers learn to distinguish between details that build a world and details that make a promise.
cards.deepDive: Because Chekhov's statements survive mainly in other people's recollections and letters, wording varies between sources, and the principle has been attributed in slightly different forms. Barthes's essay The Reality Effect (1968) is a short, stimulating counterpoint, arguing that some details in realist fiction, like a barometer in Flaubert, exist precisely because they serve no narrative function except to signal that this is the real world.

cards.title: Show, don't tell, and when to ignore it
cards.summary: Show, don't tell is perhaps the most repeated piece of writing advice. It means rendering experience through concrete action, dialogue, sensory detail and scene, so readers infer emotions and meanings, rather than stating them in summary. Instead of writing that a character was nervous, a writer might show her fiddling with her ring and checking the clock. The distinction was popularised by Percy Lubbock in The Craft of Fiction (1921), which praised Henry James's scenic method and argued that the art of fiction begins when the novelist treats the story as something to be shown. In 1961, Wayne C. Booth's The Rhetoric of Fiction challenged this orthodoxy. Booth argued that telling, the narrator's direct commentary and summary, is an essential and powerful resource, and that great novelists from Fielding to George Eliot use it brilliantly. All fiction is rhetoric, he argued, the author guiding readers' responses; the question is not whether to tell, but how well. Modern craft teachers usually agree: telling is efficient for transitions, background and compressing time, while showing is better for emotionally important moments. A novel that only shows can feel slow and opaque, while one that only tells can feel lifeless. The skill is choosing which mode to use for which moment.
cards.deepDive: Booth's book also introduced two influential concepts: the implied author, the version of the author that a text projects, distinct from the real person, and the unreliable narrator. Ursula K. Le Guin's Steering the Craft (1998) offers practical exercises that mix showing and telling and pushes back against rigid rules.

cards.title: The unreliable narrator: reading between the lies
cards.summary: An unreliable narrator is one whose account of events the reader comes to distrust. The term was coined by Wayne C. Booth in The Rhetoric of Fiction (1961), where he described a narrator as reliable when he or she speaks for or acts in accordance with the norms of the work, and unreliable when not. Unreliability comes in many forms. A narrator may be lying, as in Agatha Christie's The Murder of Roger Ackroyd (1926), whose twist provoked controversy about fair play. A narrator may be naive, like Huckleberry Finn, whose innocent descriptions expose the cruelty of the adults around him. A narrator may be self-deceiving, like Stevens the butler in Kazuo Ishiguro's The Remains of the Day (1989), whose formal, restrained language reveals by omission the love and moral failures he cannot admit. Or a narrator may be manipulative and charming, like Humbert Humbert in Vladimir Nabokov's Lolita (1955), whose elegant prose invites readers into complicity with his crimes. Unreliable narration creates a double reading: we follow the narrator's version while constructing a different story from clues, contradictions and gaps. It makes the reader an active detective and often produces dramatic irony. Later narratologists, such as Ansgar Nünning, argued that unreliability depends partly on readers' own assumptions and cultural frames.
cards.deepDive: James Phelan and Mary Patricia Martin proposed a useful typology: narrators can misreport facts, misread or misinterpret them, or misregard them in an ethical sense, and each can be underreporting rather than wrong. Their essay on The Remains of the Day is a model of close reading. Try rereading Ishiguro's opening pages with this framework in mind.

cards.title: Defamiliarisation: art makes the stone stony
cards.summary: In his 1917 essay Art as Device, sometimes translated as Art as Technique, the Russian critic Viktor Shklovsky argued that habit dulls perception. Once actions become habitual, they become automatic, and we stop truly seeing the things around us: walking, talking, even our own furniture and relationships. Shklovsky wrote that art exists to recover the sensation of life, to make the stone stony. Its method is ostranenie, usually translated as defamiliarisation or estrangement: presenting familiar things in an unfamiliar way, so that perception is slowed down and made difficult again. His favourite examples came from Leo Tolstoy, who often describes things as if seeing them for the first time, without naming them. In the story Kholstomer, the narrator is a horse, who finds human ideas about property absurd: people call him my horse, though they do not ride him or feed him. In War and Peace, an opera is described by a naive viewer as painted cardboard and people singing strangely, stripping away the conventions that make it meaningful. Shklovsky became a leading figure in Russian Formalism, which focused on literary devices rather than biography or politics. Defamiliarisation anticipates Bertolt Brecht's alienation effect in theatre, and it remains one of the best explanations of what poets and novelists do with language.
cards.deepDive: Shklovsky's essay is often included in the anthology Russian Formalist Criticism: Four Essays, translated by Lee T. Lemon and Marion J. Reis (1965). Brecht's Verfremdungseffekt, developed in the 1930s, aimed to make audiences think critically rather than identify emotionally, and the similarity in terms is not a coincidence; Brecht had contact with Russian avant-garde ideas.

cards.title: The death of the author, and the birth of the reader
cards.summary: Roland Barthes's short essay The Death of the Author, published in English in 1967 in the American magazine Aspen and in French in 1968, attacked a dominant habit of criticism: explaining a work by referring to the author's life, intentions and psychology. Barthes argued that a text is not a line of words releasing a single theological meaning, the message of an Author-God, but a multidimensional space in which a variety of writings, none of them original, blend and clash. Writing is a tissue of quotations drawn from innumerable centres of culture. Once a text is written, the author loses control over its meaning, and the unity of a text lies not in its origin but in its destination: the reader. The essay ends with the famous claim that the birth of the reader must be at the cost of the death of the Author. The argument was part of the broader shift from structuralism to post-structuralism and connected to political critiques of authority. Michel Foucault responded in 1969 with What Is an Author?, which examined the author function, how the idea of an author organises discourse and assigns responsibility. Critics such as E. D. Hirsch defended authorial intention as the standard of valid interpretation. Today most readers hold a middle position, but Barthes made it impossible to treat the author's biography as the only key.
cards.deepDive: An earlier and very different argument against relying on authors' intentions came from the American New Critics W. K. Wimsatt and Monroe Beardsley in The Intentional Fallacy (1946), which held that a poem's meaning should be judged from the text itself. Comparing it with Barthes shows how similar conclusions can come from very different theories of language and culture.

cards.title: Polyphony: Dostoevsky and the novel of many voices
cards.summary: The Russian thinker Mikhail Bakhtin argued in Problems of Dostoevsky's Art (1929), revised and expanded in 1963 as Problems of Dostoevsky's Poetics, that Fyodor Dostoevsky had invented a new kind of novel: the polyphonic novel. In most fiction, Bakhtin said, characters' voices are ultimately subordinated to the author's single vision; the author knows more and has the last word. In Dostoevsky, by contrast, there is a plurality of independent and unmerged voices and consciousnesses, each with equal rights and its own world. Characters such as Raskolnikov in Crime and Punishment or Ivan Karamazov in The Brothers Karamazov are not mouthpieces; their ideas are fully voiced, even those the author disagreed with, and the novel does not resolve their argument. Bakhtin connected this to his broader concept of dialogism: all language is shaped by previous uses and anticipated responses, and every utterance is a link in a chain of dialogue. He also developed heteroglossia, the coexistence of many social languages within a novel, and the carnivalesque, the subversive, festive inversion of hierarchies he traced in Rabelais. Bakhtin worked largely in obscurity under Stalin, and was exiled to Kazakhstan, but his ideas spread widely after the 1960s and transformed literary studies, linguistics and cultural theory.
cards.deepDive: Bakhtin's essays collected in English as The Dialogic Imagination (1981) are the best entry point to heteroglossia. His Rabelais and His World (written in the 1940s, published 1965) introduced the carnivalesque. For a lively application, read Dostoevsky's Notes from Underground (1864) with Bakhtin's idea of the word with a sideways glance: a narrator who constantly anticipates and argues with his imagined reader.

cards.title: Hemingway's iceberg: the power of what you leave out
cards.summary: Ernest Hemingway's theory of omission, often called the iceberg theory, holds that a writer can leave out important things and the story will be stronger for it, provided the writer knows what is being omitted. In Death in the Afternoon (1932), his book about bullfighting, Hemingway compared prose to an iceberg: the dignity of its movement comes from the fact that only one eighth of it is above water. If a writer knows enough about what he is writing, he can omit things he knows, and the reader will feel them as strongly as if they had been stated. But if a writer omits things because he does not know them, the result is simply hollow. Hemingway later said in interviews that he left out the war from Big Two-Hearted River (1925), a story in which a young man fishes alone; the trauma is never mentioned, yet it shapes every careful, almost ritual action. Hills Like White Elephants (1927) never names the operation the couple discusses, yet readers usually infer it. The iceberg theory owes something to Hemingway's training as a newspaper reporter at the Kansas City Star, whose style sheet demanded short sentences and vigorous English. It has influenced minimalists like Raymond Carver. The lesson for any writer is that subtext lives in the gaps, and that understatement only works when it rests on knowledge.
cards.deepDive: In his 1958 Paris Review interview, Hemingway described his practice of knowing much more than he put in. Raymond Carver's essay On Writing (1981) and the story collection What We Talk About When We Talk About Love (1981), heavily cut by his editor Gordon Lish, carry the approach to extremes, and later publication of Carver's original drafts as Beginners revealed how much had been removed.

cards.title: Flat and round characters: Forster's test
cards.summary: In Aspects of the Novel (1927), based on lectures he gave at Trinity College, Cambridge, E. M. Forster offered one of the most useful distinctions in criticism: flat and round characters. Flat characters, he said, are constructed around a single idea or quality and can be summed up in a sentence. Dickens's Mrs Micawber, who repeatedly declares she will never desert Mr Micawber, is Forster's example. Flat characters are easily recognised and remembered, and they are not necessarily a flaw: they can be comic, vivid and efficient, and Dickens's novels are crowded with them. Round characters are more complex, capable of development and contradiction. Forster's test is famous: a round character is capable of surprising in a convincing way. If it never surprises, it is flat; if it does not convince, it is flat pretending to be round. Forster considered Jane Austen a master of round characters, even her minor ones. The same book distinguishes story, a narrative of events arranged in time sequence, from plot, which emphasises causality. The king died and then the queen died is a story; the king died, and then the queen died of grief is a plot. Aspects of the Novel remains readable, witty and practical, a rare work of criticism that writers can use directly.
cards.deepDive: Forster also discusses fantasy, prophecy, pattern and rhythm in the novel, the latter being his term for repetition with variation, as in the recurring little phrase of Vinteuil's sonata in Proust. Critics have since complicated his binary; James Wood argues that flatness can be a powerful technique in its own right, and that some flat characters are more alive than round ones.

cards.title: The rise of the novel: realism, individuals and readers
cards.summary: Why did the novel emerge as a dominant form in eighteenth-century England? Ian Watt's The Rise of the Novel (1957) offered an influential answer focused on three writers: Daniel Defoe, Samuel Richardson and Henry Fielding. Watt argued that the novel was distinguished by formal realism, a set of narrative techniques that gave the impression of an authentic report of individual experience. Unlike earlier romances and epics, which used traditional plots and types, novels such as Robinson Crusoe (1719) and Pamela (1740) featured particular individuals with ordinary names, placed in specific times and places, whose lives unfolded through cause and effect. Watt connected this to broader changes: philosophical individualism and empiricism from Descartes and Locke; the rise of Protestant introspection and diary keeping; economic individualism, of which Crusoe is a famous parable; and the growth of a middle-class reading public, especially women, with more leisure, circulating libraries and a booming print trade. Later critics challenged Watt's narrow focus on English male authors, pointing to earlier women novelists such as Aphra Behn and Eliza Haywood, to the long tradition of prose fiction in other cultures, and to the wider European picture. Still, Watt's question, what social changes made the novel possible, remains central to literary history.
cards.deepDive: Margaret Anne Doody's The True Story of the Novel (1996) argues the novel is far older, tracing it to ancient Greek and Roman prose fiction. Michael McKeon's The Origins of the English Novel, 1600-1740 (1987) offers a more dialectical account. For a global counterpoint, consider The Tale of Genji, written in Japan around 1000 AD, often called the first novel.

cards.title: Does reading fiction make you more empathetic?
cards.summary: The idea that literature cultivates empathy is old, but in recent decades psychologists have tried to test it. Keith Oatley and Raymond Mar argued that fiction works as a simulation of social experience: just as flight simulators train pilots, stories let readers practise understanding other minds. In correlational studies, people who read more fiction tended to score higher on measures of theory of mind and empathy, though such associations could reflect who chooses to read. In 2013, David Kidd and Emanuele Castano published a widely reported experiment in Science. Participants who read short excerpts of literary fiction, by authors such as Don DeLillo and Louise Erdrich, performed better immediately afterwards on tests of theory of mind, such as the Reading the Mind in the Eyes Test, than those who read popular fiction, non-fiction or nothing. The study received enormous attention. However, a 2016 replication attempt by Maria Eugenia Panero and colleagues, involving several labs and a larger sample, did not reproduce the effect of a single brief reading session. Later meta-analyses suggest that fiction reading may have small positive effects on social cognition, but that the evidence is mixed and effect sizes are modest. The more robust finding is the correlation between lifetime reading and social cognition, whose direction of causality is still uncertain.
cards.deepDive: Dodell-Feder and Tamir's 2018 meta-analysis found a small but statistically significant effect of fiction reading on social cognition across experiments, while warning of publication bias. Kidd and Castano responded to failed replications with further studies. Keith Oatley's Such Stuff as Dreams (2011) is an accessible account of fiction as simulation.

cards.title: Narrative transportation: why stories persuade
cards.summary: In 2000, Melanie Green and Timothy Brock introduced the concept of narrative transportation in the Journal of Personality and Social Psychology. Transportation is the experience of being absorbed into a story, a combination of attention, imagery and emotion in which readers lose track of their surroundings. Green and Brock developed a scale to measure it, asking people how much they could picture events, how much they wanted to learn how the story ended, and whether they felt emotionally involved. In their experiments, participants who were more transported by a story, such as one about a young girl murdered by a psychiatric patient at a shopping mall, were more likely to adopt beliefs consistent with the story and less likely to find faults in it, even when the story was labelled fiction. Transportation seems to persuade through different routes from arguments. Absorbed readers are less inclined to counter-argue, they identify with characters, and the story's events feel like experience rather than claims. This helps explain the power of narrative in advertising, health communication, political messaging and misinformation. A 2014 meta-analysis by Tom van Laer and colleagues confirmed that transportation predicts changes in attitudes and intentions across studies. The practical lesson cuts both ways: a good story is a strong tool for teaching and a strong tool for manipulation.
cards.deepDive: Green and Brock's transportation-imagery model connects to earlier work by Richard Gerrig, whose Experiencing Narrative Worlds (1993) used the metaphor of travel to describe reading. Health researchers have used narrative interventions, for example stories about cancer screening, with some success, though narrative persuasion also makes false information harder to correct.

cards.title: Orwell's rules: bad prose and bad politics
cards.summary: George Orwell's essay Politics and the English Language, published in the magazine Horizon in 1946, argues that the decline of a language has political and economic causes, but that bad language also enables bad thinking. Orwell collected examples of what he considered sloppy contemporary prose and identified recurring faults: dying metaphors used without thought, pretentious diction, meaningless words and verbal false limbs that pad sentences. Most seriously, he argued that political language is designed to make lies sound truthful and murder respectable. Euphemism allows people to name terrible things without calling up mental pictures of them; he gave examples such as pacification for bombing villages and driving out inhabitants. Orwell ended the essay with six rules. In summary: never use a metaphor, simile or figure of speech you are used to seeing in print; never use a long word where a short one will do; if it is possible to cut a word out, always cut it out; never use the passive where you can use the active; never use a foreign phrase, scientific word or jargon if you can think of an everyday equivalent; and break any of these rules sooner than say anything outright barbarous. The last rule matters: Orwell framed them as aids to thinking clearly, not mechanical laws.
cards.deepDive: Linguists have pointed out that Orwell breaks his own rules in the essay, including using the passive voice often, and that some of his examples are unfair. Geoffrey Pullum has criticised the anti-passive advice found in Orwell and Strunk and White. The essay's connection to Newspeak in Nineteen Eighty-Four (1949), published three years later, is direct and worth tracing.

cards.title: The curse of knowledge and classic style
cards.summary: In The Sense of Style (2014), the cognitive psychologist Steven Pinker argues that the single best explanation of why good people write bad prose is the curse of knowledge: once you know something, it is very hard to imagine what it is like not to know it. Experts forget that readers do not share their jargon, abbreviations and background assumptions. The term comes from economics: in 1989 Colin Camerer, George Loewenstein and Martin Weber showed that better-informed traders could not ignore their private knowledge when predicting the judgements of less-informed traders, even when it would have paid them to do so. A memorable demonstration came from Elizabeth Newton's 1990 Stanford dissertation: people asked to tap the rhythm of a well-known song, such as Happy Birthday, predicted listeners would identify around half the songs, but listeners identified only about 2.5 per cent. The tappers could hear the melody in their heads; the listeners heard only knocks. Pinker's remedy is classic style, a concept he borrows from Francis-Noël Thomas and Mark Turner's Clear and Simple as the Truth (1994). In classic style, the writer acts as a guide directing the reader's gaze to something in the world, as in a conversation between equals. The best practical defence is to show drafts to people outside your field.
cards.deepDive: Pinker's book also defends some traditional rules and rejects others, including many prohibitions in usage guides such as the ban on split infinitives. Thomas and Turner's book contrasts classic style with plain, practical, reflexive and prophetic styles. The Newton tapping study is described in Chip and Dan Heath's Made to Stick (2007).

cards.title: Stream of consciousness: from William James to Woolf
cards.summary: The phrase stream of consciousness comes from psychology before it entered literature. In The Principles of Psychology (1890), William James argued that consciousness does not appear to itself chopped up in bits; it is nothing jointed, it flows. A river or a stream, he said, are the metaphors by which it is most naturally described. In the early twentieth century, novelists tried to capture this flow on the page. Dorothy Richardson's Pilgrimage sequence, beginning in 1915, was described by the novelist May Sinclair in 1918 as stream of consciousness, the first application of the term to fiction. James Joyce's Ulysses (1922) pushed the technique to extremes, culminating in Molly Bloom's final monologue, eight enormous unpunctuated sentences. Virginia Woolf, in her essay Modern Fiction, urged writers to record the atoms as they fall upon the mind in the order in which they fall, and in Mrs Dalloway (1925) and To the Lighthouse (1927) she moved fluidly between characters' minds, using free indirect style rather than raw interior monologue. William Faulkner's The Sound and the Fury (1929) opens with the fragmented perceptions of Benjy, a cognitively disabled man, whose section disorients readers. The technique reflected modernist interest in subjectivity, time and memory, influenced by James, Henri Bergson and Freud.
cards.deepDive: Critics distinguish between stream of consciousness as a subject, the representation of mental flow, and interior monologue as a technique, direct quotation of a character's thoughts. Édouard Dujardin's Les Lauriers sont coupés (1887), which Joyce acknowledged as an influence, is an early example. Robert Humphrey's Stream of Consciousness in the Modern Novel (1954) is a classic study.

cards.title: The objective correlative: emotion through things
cards.summary: In his 1919 essay Hamlet and His Problems, T. S. Eliot made a provocative claim: Shakespeare's Hamlet, far from being a masterpiece, was most certainly an artistic failure. His reason introduced one of the most famous terms in twentieth-century criticism. The only way of expressing emotion in the form of art, Eliot argued, is by finding an objective correlative, a set of objects, a situation, a chain of events which shall be the formula of that particular emotion, so that when the external facts are given, the emotion is immediately evoked. Eliot's examples came from Macbeth, where Lady Macbeth's sleepwalking scene gives her state of mind through concrete details. In Hamlet, by contrast, Eliot argued that the prince's disgust exceeds anything the plot provides: his mother's remarriage is not an adequate correlative for the intensity of his feeling, so the emotion seems inexpressible and baffling. Many critics reject the judgement of Hamlet, and the phrase itself had been used earlier by the American painter Washington Allston. But the idea has been enormously useful for writers. Instead of naming emotions, find the concrete objects and events that will carry them, like the shoes in a tragedy or the empty chair at the table. It is a sharper version of show, don't tell.
cards.deepDive: Eliot's poetry applies the idea: The Love Song of J. Alfred Prufrock (1915) communicates paralysis and anxiety through images of evening sky, half-deserted streets and coffee spoons, rather than direct statement. Eliot's essay appears in The Sacred Wood (1920), which is in the public domain and available free online.
